runs.answer:
**The verified data show changes in climate conditions and conservation practices over time, but they do not establish a correlation between them.** That is an evidence limitation—not evidence that no relationship exists.

### What the historical observations show

| Series | Geography and period | Verified observations |
|---|---|---|
| Annual average temperature | Maryland, 1985–2012 | 54.8°F in 1985; 57.5°F in 2012—a **2.7°F endpoint increase** |
| Annual precipitation | Maryland, 1985–2012 | 40.69 inches in 1985; 40.40 in 2012, with substantial variation between years—for example, 60.74 inches in 2003 |
| Estimated cover-crop area | Chesapeake watershed, 2002 and 2012 | Increased from **481.5 to 1,770.6 km²** |
| Estimated conservation-tillage area | Chesapeake watershed, 1985, 1992, 2002, 2012 | Fell from **8,077.0 km²** in 1985 to **7,057.3 km²** in 1992, then rose to **8,403.1 km²** in 2012 |

Sources: NOAA NCEI’s Maryland [temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/18/tavg/12/12/1985-2012.csv) and [precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/18/pcp/12/12/1985-2012.csv) series (catalog ID **C00005**); USGS/Chesapeake Bay Program, [*Implementation of conservation tillage and cover crops…*](https://doi.org/10.5066/P9SRZS8P), identifier **USGS_5b3bb606e4b040769c18bdc9**.

### Why these do not demonstrate correlation

- **Geography differs:** Maryland statewide climate cannot be directly paired with practices across the entire Chesapeake watershed.
- **Practice observations are sparse:** cover crops have only two observation years and tillage four; missing years cannot be filled in as observations.
- **Endpoint differences are not trends.** The temperature comparison above is not an estimated warming trend, and annual precipitation totals do not describe seasonal timing or extremes.
- **Area is not adoption rate:** practice figures are spatially allocated estimates, not direct measurements at every catchment or percentages of farms adopting a practice. Cover-crop and tillage areas can overlap.
- These practices were reported for **soil and water-quality management**, not demonstrated climate-driven adoption. Even a valid correlation would not establish causation.

### Other relevant evidence and availability

A targeted catalog search returned five candidates; three were assessed. By keyword relevance, they ordered as: [conservation-practice physical effects](https://doi.org/10.5066/P9VY95KT), the implementation dataset above, then [water-quality trends in agricultural watersheds](https://doi.org/10.23719/1531764). This is not a ranking of scientific strength.

**Availability differs:** only the implementation dataset has verified, narrowly scoped historical observations here. The alternatives’ access routes remain unverified; observation periods and dictionaries were not supplied. Catalog listings advertise XML metadata or DOI links, not confirmed analysis-ready files. Public-access labels do not resolve all usage terms.

**Bottom line:** a defensible correlation study would require climate and practice observations matched to the same geography and years. The available historical snapshots support descriptive context, not a correlation coefficient or climate-attribution claim.

datasets.title: Characterization of the Impact of Agricultural Conservation Practices on Natural Resource Concerns in the Chesapeake Bay Watershed
datasets.description: The U.S. Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) provides funding and technical assistance for the implementation of practices that enable people to conserve, maintain, or improve soil, water, and related natural resources. NRCS conservation practices, or best management practices, relate the conservation practices to conservation practice physical effects (CPPE). Physical effects are listed in the data and purpose and include effects such as nutrients and pesticides transported to surface and/or groundwater. The CPPE is published in the NRCS Field Office Technical Guide and is listed in the sources section. NRCS's CPPE includes a limited set of practices. All practices that do not have an NRCS-assigned CPPE were evaluated using NRCS practice standard criteria and required enhancements to determine the most comparable practice that with an assigned CPPE. The CPPE categories are ranked on a scale of -5 to +5. These rankings are categorical and indicate a range from substantial worsening (-5) to substantial improvement (+5) with zero indicating no effect. NRCS conservation practice data are available to USGS researchers via a data sharing agreement.

datasets.title: Implementation of conservation tillage and cover crops in the Chesapeake Bay watershed, 1985 to 2012
datasets.description: Conservation tillage practices and cover crops are used throughout the Chesapeake Bay watershed to reduce soil loss and improve water quality. Implementation of these Best Management Practices (BMPs) were reported to the Chesapeake Bay Program (CBP) by each state in the watershed (New York, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Delaware, West Virginia, and Virginia). Estimates of acres of implementation per CBP land river modeling segment for the years 1985 through 2014 were provided to the U.S. Geological Survey. These data were distributed to agricultural land use cells in the National Land Cover Dataset (NLCD) dataset and summed for National Hydrography Dataset (NHD) Plus version 1 catchments to provide estimates of implementation at spatial scales commonly used for modeling purposes for the years 1985, 1992, 2002, and 2012 for conservation tillage, as well as 2002 and 2012 for cover crops.
